FOR CUSTOM FARM OPERATORS

A per-acre rate that starts from your machine, not a rumor.

Custom rate surveys report what other operators charged last season, on someone else's machine. This free calculator works out the rate a job actually needs to cover on yours — field capacity, fuel, repairs, the machine's own ownership cost spread over the hours it runs, and your labor — then checks a season of jobs against an income goal.

Wondering why the same job needs a different rate on a machine that sits idle more? See why a lightly used machine needs a higher rate for a worked example.

Private by default

Everything on this page runs in your browser. Your job figures and season list are never uploaded, there is no account, and nothing is saved when you close the tab. We count only anonymous local feature events (job-priced, season-check) so we can tell whether the calculator gets used — no acres, rates, or profit figures are recorded, and Do Not Track / Global Privacy Control turn it off automatically.

Common questions

Why does the field efficiency percentage matter so much?

Because it directly scales how many hours a job actually takes. A machine rated for a given speed and width never works at 100% of that in the field — turns at the end of every pass, overlap between passes, and stops to refill or unload all eat into it. Overstating field efficiency understates hours for the job, which understates every cost that scales with hours: fuel, repairs, ownership cost, and your own labor.

Why spread the machine's ownership cost over hours used per year instead of just this job's hours?

A combine or planter costs money to own — depreciation, interest, insurance, and housing — whether it runs 50 hours a year or 500. Spreading that fixed annual cost over the hours it actually runs, then charging each job its share of the resulting per-hour figure, is what makes lightly used equipment carry a higher rate per acre than the same machine run hard across more acres and more customers.

Is margin here a percentage of cost or a percentage of price?

A percentage of price. Fifteen percent margin on a $3,000 job is $450 of profit; a 15% mark-up on $3,000 of cost is $450 too, coincidentally, but the two diverge as the margin percentage rises — a 40% margin and a 40% mark-up are very different numbers. This calculator always treats your target as a share of what you bill, since that is the number a season's revenue and profit actually depend on.

Does this replace a published custom rate survey?

No. Published regional custom rate surveys report what other operators charged last season, averaged across many farms and machines — useful as a market check, not as your own cost structure. This calculator works out what a job costs a machine with your specific speed, width, fuel burn, repair history, ownership cost, and hours of annual use, which the survey average cannot know. See this calculator vs. a published custom rate survey for more.

Is my data uploaded anywhere?

No. Every field on this page runs in your browser only. Nothing is sent to a server, there is no account, and the job list you type into the season section is never saved anywhere — it exists only in the page while it is open. Usage counting only tallies anonymous feature events, and you can turn it off with the button above.

vs-survey-rates.html.text:
← Custom farm rate calculator

This calculator vs. a published custom rate survey

Several state extension services and farm publications run a regional custom rate survey: they ask operators what they charged for a job last season and publish the average, often broken out by region and by task (combining, planting, spraying, baling, tillage). That average is a genuinely useful market check — it tells you roughly what a customer in your area expects to pay. It does not know your machine.

A survey figure is computed from many operators' costs, not yours. Field capacity depends on your own speed, implement width, and field efficiency. Fuel and repairs scale with the hours a job takes on your machine, at your fuel price and your own repair history. Ownership cost — depreciation, interest, insurance, housing — is fixed for the year, so a machine run hard across many customers spreads that fixed cost over more acres than the same machine used lightly, and the two operators need different rates even doing the identical job. A single regional average cannot carry that difference; this calculator is built entirely from it.

QuestionWhere to answer it
What do operators in my region typically charge for this task? A published regional custom rate survey.
Is my quote roughly in line with the going rate, if a customer asks? A published survey, as a sanity check.
What does this job cost my specific machine, at my fuel price and my hours? This calculator's per-job rate — a survey has no way to know your machine's numbers.
Does a season of jobs at this rate hit my income goal? This calculator's season rollup — a survey reports one job's average, not a season.
How much is my rate driven by ownership cost I'm not spreading over enough hours? This calculator's ownership-cost breakdown — a survey average bakes this in for someone else's usage, not yours.
Price your own job

This tool needs no account, upload, or subscription: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and your machine numbers and season list stay on your device — nothing is uploaded anywhere, and refreshing the page clears the season table on purpose.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or a published custom rate survey?

Use both, for different questions. A survey (such as a state extension service's regional custom rate survey) tells you what other operators charged last season, averaged across many farms, machines, and conditions — a useful market check on whether your number is in the right neighborhood. It cannot know your own machine's field speed, width, field efficiency, fuel burn, repair history, or how many hours you actually spread its ownership cost over. This calculator answers that second question: what does this specific job cost your specific machine, this year.

Why not just charge the survey average?

A survey average can be right for you by coincidence, but it is computed from someone else's costs. A machine run hard across many customers spreads its fixed ownership cost over more acres than a machine used lightly, so the same survey figure undercharges one operator and overcharges the other. Fuel price, local repair costs, and your own field efficiency also move the real number away from a regional average in either direction.

Does this calculator replace a survey?

No. A survey is still a useful sanity check and a reference point when a customer asks how your number compares to the going rate. This calculator does not collect or aggregate anyone else's rates and is not a substitute for that market context — it only computes your own cost-based number from figures you supply.

Is this page affiliated with any particular survey publisher?

No. This page does not name or link to any specific survey publisher, and makes no claim about any survey's published figures. It describes custom rate surveys as a category to explain when to use each tool.

why-a-lightly-used-machine-needs-a-highe.text:
← Custom farm rate calculator

Why does a lightly used machine need a higher custom rate?

Two operators with the same combine, doing the same 160-acre job at the same speed, width, fuel price, and repair cost, can need very different per-acre rates to hit the same margin. The difference is not the job — it is how many hours the machine runs across the whole year. Ownership cost is fixed for the year; hours used per year decides how thin or thick it gets spread.

Open the free custom farm rate calculator

What stays the same, what changes

The job itself doesn't change. 160 acres, 4.5 mph, a 30-foot header, 75% field efficiency, $3.85/gal fuel at 12 gal/hr, $18/hr in repairs, $24/hr labor, and a 15% target margin — identical on both machines. What differs is hours used per year: one machine runs 250 hours across the season and every customer's ground, the other only 100.

Ownership cost per hour is the fixed annual cost divided by those hours. A $28,000-a-year machine costs $112.00 an hour to own when it runs 250 hours, and $280.00 an hour — two and a half times as much — when it only runs 100. Every job that machine does then carries that higher per-hour figure for however long the job takes.

Worked example

Figure250 hrs/year100 hrs/year
Ownership cost per hour$112.00$280.00
Hours for this 160-acre job13.0 hrs13.0 hrs
Fuel cost$602.31$602.31
Repairs & maintenance$234.67$234.67
Ownership cost (this job's share)$1,460.15$3,650.37
Labor cost$312.89$312.89
Total cost$2,610.01$4,800.24
Break-even rate$16.31/ac$30.00/ac
Rate at 15% target margin$19.19/ac$35.30/ac

Fuel, repairs, and labor are identical in both columns — the field capacity, speed, and job size never changed. Only the ownership-cost line moved, and it alone is enough to push the per-acre rate up 84%. A published custom rate survey cannot see this: it reports one number per job type, not what a specific machine's annual utilization does to that number.

Common questions

Why does a lightly used machine need a higher per-acre rate for the same job?

Because annual ownership cost — depreciation, interest, insurance, and housing — is a fixed dollar figure for the year regardless of how many hours the machine actually runs. Dividing that fixed cost by fewer hours produces a higher ownership cost per hour, and that higher per-hour figure gets charged against every job in proportion to how long it takes, whether the job itself is any different or not.

How much does hours used per year actually change the rate?

On a 160-acre job with identical field speed, width, fuel, and repair costs, a machine used 250 hours a year needs about $19.19 per acre to hit a 15% margin. The same machine, same job, used only 100 hours a year needs about $35.30 per acre — 84% more — because its $28,000 annual ownership cost is spread over 150 fewer hours.

What counts toward hours used per year?

Every hour the machine runs across the whole year — your own ground and every paying customer's field work combined, not just the hours on the job you are pricing right now. A machine that also covers 400 acres of your own ground before it ever does custom work for hire has a much lower ownership cost per hour than one that only leaves the shed for a handful of custom jobs.

Is my data uploaded anywhere?

No. Every field on the calculator runs in your browser only. Nothing is sent to a server, there is no account, and nothing you type is saved anywhere — it exists only in the page while it is open. Usage counting only tallies anonymous feature events, and you can turn it off from the calculator's own page.
